parent_const_preamble.title: Preamble to the Constitution of India
parent_const_preamble.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Preamble - Preamble to the Constitution of India
PART: Preamble | CATEGORY: Foundational Principles
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: The Preamble serves as the preface to the Indian Constitution, outlining its core philosophy, values, objectives, and source of authority (the people of India). As established in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368, provided the basic features are not destroyed.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Drafted by the Constituent Assembly, influenced by Jawaharlal Nehru's Objectives Resolution of 1946. The words 'SOCIALIST', 'SECULAR', and 'INTEGRITY' were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
parent_const_preamble.raw_text: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

As established in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368, provided the basic features are not destroyed.

parent_const_art_001.title: Name and territory of the Union
parent_const_art_001.part: Part I - The Union and its Territory
parent_const_art_001.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 1 - Name and territory of the Union
PART: Part I - The Union and its Territory | CATEGORY: Territorial Sovereignty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. The territory of India shall comprise: the territories of the States, Union territories specified in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes India as an indestructible Union composed of destructible states, emphasizing unity over contractual federation.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Debated in the Constituent Assembly on September 18, 1949, balancing traditional heritage ('Bharat') with modern international nomenclature ('India').

The territory of India shall comprise: the territories of the States, Union territories specified in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired.

parent_const_art_002.title: Admission or establishment of new States
parent_const_art_002.part: Part I - The Union and its Territory
parent_const_art_002.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 2 - Admission or establishment of new States
PART: Part I - The Union and its Territory | CATEGORY: Territorial Sovereignty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Vests plenary power in Parliament to admit external territories or establish new states not previously part of the Indian Union, such as the admission of Sikkim in 1975.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Differentiates admission of foreign territories (Article 2) from reorganization of internal states (Article 3).

parent_const_art_003.title: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
parent_const_art_003.part: Part I - The Union and its Territory
parent_const_art_003.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 3 - Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
PART: Part I - The Union and its Territory | CATEGORY: Territorial Sovereignty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament may by law form a new State by separation of territory, increase or diminish state areas, alter boundaries or names of existing States, provided the bill is recommended by the President and referred to the affected State Legislature for views.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Empowers Parliament to reorganize internal state boundaries. The opinion of the state legislature is advisory and not binding on Parliament.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Used for historical reorganizations: States Reorganisation Act 1956, creation of Andhra (1953), Gujarat/Maharashtra (1960), and Telangana (2014).

parent_const_art_004.title: Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for amendment of First and Fourth Schedules
parent_const_art_004.part: Part I - The Union and its Territory
parent_const_art_004.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 4 - Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for amendment of First and Fourth Schedules
PART: Part I - The Union and its Territory | CATEGORY: Territorial Sovereignty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Laws made under articles 2 and 3 provide for amendment of First and Fourth Schedules and shall not be deemed amendments of the Constitution under Article 368.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Ensures state creation and boundary changes require only a simple majority in Parliament, exempting them from the special majority requirements of Article 368.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: In Berubari Union Reference (1960), the Supreme Court clarified that ceding Indian territory to a foreign power requires an amendment under Article 368, not ordinary law under Article 3/4.

parent_const_art_005.title: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
parent_const_art_005.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 5 - Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
PART: Part II - Citizenship | CATEGORY: Citizenship
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: At the commencement of this Constitution every person who has domicile in India and was born in India, whose parents were born in India, or who resided for not less than 5 years shall be a citizen.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Defines citizenship at the moment the Constitution came into effect on January 26, 1950, based on domicile combined with birth, parentage, or residence.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Addressed partition dislocations while establishing secular, non-discriminatory citizenship principles.

parent_const_art_009.title: Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
parent_const_art_009.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 9 - Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
PART: Part II - Citizenship | CATEGORY: Citizenship
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No person shall be a citizen of India if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes the fundamental principle of single citizenship in India, prohibiting dual citizenship under constitutional law.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Rejected dual allegiance to preserve national unity and sovereignty post-independence.

parent_const_art_009.explanation: Establishes the fundamental principle of single citizenship in India, prohibiting dual citizenship under constitutional law.

parent_const_art_011.title: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
parent_const_art_011.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 11 - Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
PART: Part II - Citizenship | CATEGORY: Citizenship
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Nothing in this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make provisions with respect to acquisition and termination of citizenship and related matters.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Gives Parliament comprehensive authority over citizenship matters, under which the Citizenship Act, 1955 and subsequent amendments were enacted.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: The framers intentionally deferred long-term citizenship policy to elected legislatures.

parent_const_art_012.title: Definition of State
parent_const_art_012.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 12 - Definition of State
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 12 defines what institutions are bound by Fundamental Rights. The phrase 'other authorities' has been expansively interpreted by the Supreme Court in Ajay Hasia (1981) and Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) using the test of deep and pervasive state control.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Drafted by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar to ensure that all organs exercising public power or state function are subjected to constitutional limitations.

parent_const_art_013.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
parent_const_art_013.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 13 - Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: All laws in force inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void to extent of inconsistency. State shall not make laws abridging rights. Law includes ordinances, rules, customs having force of law. Clause (4) states Article 13 does not apply to Article 368 amendments.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutes the express foundation of Judicial Review in India. Incorporates the Doctrine of Severability and Doctrine of Eclipse.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Clause (4) was inserted by the 24th Amendment (1971) to counter the Golak Nath (1967) ruling. Kesavananda Bharati upheld clause (4) subject to the Basic Structure Doctrine.

parent_const_art_014.title: Equality before law
parent_const_art_014.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 14 - Equality before law
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Combines British common-law 'Equality before the law' (absence of arbitrary privilege) with American 14th Amendment 'Equal protection of the laws' (equal treatment in equal circumstances). Prohibits arbitrary state action under the doctrine established in E.P. Royappa (1974) and Maneka Gandhi (1978).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Applies to 'any person', extending equality rights to non-citizens, legal corporations, and statutory entities.

parent_const_art_015.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
parent_const_art_015.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 15 - Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall not discriminate against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Guarantees equal access to shops, public restaurants, wells, and places of public resort. Empowers State to make special provisions for women, children, backward classes, SCs/STs, and economically weaker sections (EWS).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guarantees substantive equality. Clause (4) was added by 1st Amendment (1951) after Champakam Dorairajan; Clause (5) by 93rd Amendment (2005); Clause (6) by 103rd Amendment (2019) introducing 10% EWS reservation.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Specifically crafted to dismantle horizontal social discrimination and untouchability in public accommodations.

parent_const_art_016.title: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
parent_const_art_016.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 16 - Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Guarantees equality of opportunity for citizens in public employment. Prohibits discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence. Enables reservations for backward classes not adequately represented (4), reservations in promotion for SC/ST with consequential seniority (4A), and 10% EWS reservation (6).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutes the foundation of affirmative action jurisprudence in Indian civil service, examined in landmark rulings Indra Sawhney (1992), M. Nagaraj (2006), and Jarnail Singh (2018).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Drafted to reconcile individual merit with social justice and representative governance.

parent_const_art_017.title: Abolition of Untouchability
parent_const_art_017.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 17 - Abolition of Untouchability
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: 'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Absolute fundamental right without exceptions. Operates against both the State and private individuals. Implemented via the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: A historic moral imperative of the Indian freedom movement led by Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

parent_const_art_018.title: Abolition of titles
parent_const_art_018.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 18 - Abolition of titles
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No title, not being military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. No citizen shall accept titles from foreign States.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Abolishes feudal and colonial titles (e.g. Rai Bahadur, Sir). In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court held that National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) are decorations and not hereditary titles within Article 18.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Designed to establish a republican egalitarian society devoid of artificial noble classes.

parent_const_art_019.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
parent_const_art_019.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 19 - Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Guarantees six fundamental freedoms to citizens: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, associations/unions, free movement, residence, and trade/profession. Subject to reasonable restrictions under clauses (2) to (6) for sovereignty, security, public order, and morality.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Core charter of civil liberties. Freedom of speech encompasses freedom of the press (Bennett Coleman, 1973), right to internet access (Anuradha Bhasin, 2020), and online expression (Shreya Singhal, 2015). Restrictions must satisfy proportionality.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Clause (1)(f) guaranteeing right to property was deleted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

parent_const_art_020.title: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
parent_const_art_020.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 20 - Protection in respect of conviction for offences
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Protects against ex-post facto penal laws (1), double jeopardy (2), and self-incrimination (3). Cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency under Article 359.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court ruled that involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph tests, and brain mapping violate Article 20(3) and personal liberty under Article 21.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Non-derogable right safeguarded by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 following Emergency abuses.

parent_const_art_021.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
parent_const_art_021.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 21 - Protection of life and personal liberty
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: The heart of fundamental rights. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Supreme Court held that 'procedure established by law' must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating American procedural and substantive due process. In Puttaswamy (2017), a 9-judge bench unanimously declared the Right to Privacy an intrinsic part of Article 21. Also encompasses right to livelihood (Olga Tellis), clean environment (M.C. Mehta), healthcare, and dignity.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Cannot be suspended during emergency (44th Amendment). Replaced draft term 'due process of law' following B.N. Rau's discussions with US Justice Felix Frankfurter, but reclaimed due process through judicial interpretation.

parent_const_art_021a.title: Right to education
parent_const_art_021a.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 21A - Right to education
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Enforces free and compulsory elementary education as an actionable fundamental right, operationalized through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, elevating Directive Principle Article 45 into a Fundamental Right following Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993).

parent_const_art_022.title: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
parent_const_art_022.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 22 - Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Guarantees grounds of arrest, right to legal counsel, production before nearest magistrate within 24 hours. Regulates preventive detention, mandating Advisory Boards for detention exceeding statutory periods.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes procedural safeguards against arbitrary arrest, amplified by the Supreme Court's binding arrest guidelines in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Constitutes a unique constitutional regulation of preventive detention in peacetime democracy.

parent_const_art_023.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
parent_const_art_023.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 23 - Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Traffic in human beings, begar, and forced labour are prohibited and punishable by law. State may impose non-discriminatory compulsory public service.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: In PUDR v. Union of India (Asiad Workers Case, 1982), the Supreme Court ruled that paying less than minimum wage constitutes forced labour under Article 23.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Erased centuries of bonded labour, caste-mandated unpaid labour (begar), and feudal servitude.

parent_const_art_024.title: Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
parent_const_art_024.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 24 - Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Absolute fundamental right protecting children against economic exploitation and industrial hazards, reinforced by M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (Sivakasi Child Labour Case, 1996).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Reflects the constitutional commitment to child welfare, health, and dignity.

parent_const_art_025.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
parent_const_art_025.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 25 - Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: All persons are entitled to freedom of conscience and right to profess, practice, and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, and health. State may regulate secular aspects and enact social reform.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guarantees religious liberty to individuals. The Supreme Court developed the 'Essential Religious Practices' doctrine in Shirur Mutt (1954) to determine which rituals are protected, applied in Shayara Bano (2017) and Sabarimala (2018).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Guarantees rights to both citizens and non-citizens, affirming positive secularism.

parent_const_art_026.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
parent_const_art_026.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 26 - Freedom to manage religious affairs
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Every religious denomination has right to establish institutions, manage religious affairs, own property, and administer property in accordance with law, subject to public order, morality, and health.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Protects collective religious rights of denominations. Unlike Article 25, Article 26 is not subject to other fundamental rights in Part III, though administration of secular property is subject to state law.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Ensured that temples, maths, mosques, churches, and gurudwaras enjoy institutional autonomy.

parent_const_art_027.title: Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
parent_const_art_027.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 27 - Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No person shall be compelled to pay taxes specifically appropriated for promotion or maintenance of any particular religion.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Prohibits the state from levying religious taxes (such as historical Jizya). Differentiates between a tax (prohibited) and a regulatory fee for administering religious trusts (permissible under Shirur Mutt).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Affirms secular fiscal neutrality of the Indian Republic.

parent_const_art_028.title: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
parent_const_art_028.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 28 - Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds. Voluntary participation in state-aided institutions.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Ensures secular public education while safeguarding individual conscience from compulsory indoctrination.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Distinguishes between wholly state-funded institutions (prohibited), trusts administered by state (permitted), and state-aided institutions (voluntary).

parent_const_art_029.title: Protection of interests of minorities
parent_const_art_029.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 29 - Protection of interests of minorities
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Citizens with distinct language, script, or culture have right to conserve the same. No denial of admission to state-aided educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, or language.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Clause (1) protects linguistic, cultural, and script diversity for any section of citizens, while Clause (2) guarantees individual non-discrimination in state-aided education.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Broadened beyond religious minorities to protect all cultural and linguistic communities across India.

parent_const_art_030.title: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
parent_const_art_030.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 30 - Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Religious and linguistic minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice without state discrimination in financial aid.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Interpreted in landmark 11-judge bench ruling T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) and P.A. Inamdar (2005) balancing minority institutional autonomy with general academic regulatory standards.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Vested solemn constitutional trust in minority communities to preserve their cultural and educational heritage.

parent_const_art_031b.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
parent_const_art_031b.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 31B - Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule are immunized from constitutional challenge on grounds of inconsistency with Part III Fundamental Rights.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Created the Ninth Schedule protective umbrella. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a 9-judge bench ruled that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) are open to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 to insulate agrarian land reform and zamindari abolition legislation from judicial invalidation.

parent_const_art_031c.title: Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
parent_const_art_031c.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 31C - Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Protects laws giving effect to Directive Principles (specifically Articles 39(b) and 39(c)) against challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a Basic Feature of the Constitution, striking down the 42nd Amendment's blanket protection.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by 25th Amendment (1971); partially struck down in Kesavananda Bharati, and narrowed in Minerva Mills.

parent_const_art_032.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
parent_const_art_032.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 32 - Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Guarantees right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Supreme Court empowered to issue writs of Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. Right shall not be suspended except as provided by Constitution.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. Unlike Article 226, the right to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a guaranteed Fundamental Right. Formed the foundation for Public Interest Litigation (PIL) expanding locus standi.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: During the 1975-77 Emergency, ADM Jabalpur suspended writ remedies, which was firmly overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).

parent_const_art_033.title: Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc.
parent_const_art_033.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 33 - Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc.
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament may by law restrict or abrogate Fundamental Rights in application to Armed Forces, police forces, and intelligence agencies to ensure discipline and proper duty discharge.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Authorizes statutory restrictions on speech, association, and unionization for military, paramilitary, and police forces.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Ensures discipline and political neutrality of national armed services.

parent_const_art_034.title: Restriction on rights conferred by this Part while martial law is in force in any area
parent_const_art_034.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 34 - Restriction on rights conferred by this Part while martial law is in force in any area
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament may indemnify persons for acts done in connection with restoration of order where martial law was in force.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Provides constitutional sanction for Acts of Indemnity following periods of military rule or martial law.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Derived from British constitutional conventions on martial law indemnities.

parent_const_art_035.title: Legislation to give effect to the provisions of this Part
parent_const_art_035.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 35 - Legislation to give effect to the provisions of this Part
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Right
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament has exclusive power (denying power to State Legislatures) to make laws prescribing punishments for offences under Article 17 (untouchability) and Article 23 (human trafficking/forced labour).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guarantees nationwide uniformity in penal laws enforcing fundamental rights.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Prevented fragmented state-level penalties for heinous caste and human rights violations.

parent_const_art_036.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_036.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 36 - Definition of State in Part IV
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: In this Part, unless context otherwise requires, 'the State' has same meaning as in Part III (Article 12).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Extends the comprehensive definition of State across all governmental organs to the pursuit of Directive Principles.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Links welfare obligations directly to all state and local authorities.

parent_const_art_037.title: Application of the principles contained in this Part
parent_const_art_037.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_037.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 37 - Application of the principles contained in this Part
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Directive principles are not enforceable by courts, but are fundamental in the governance of the country, and it is the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes the non-justiciable yet fundamental character of socio-economic rights. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Supreme Court held that Part III and Part IV are complementary, forming the conscience of the Constitution.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Modeled after the Irish Constitution's Directive Principles of Social Policy.

parent_const_art_038.title: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
parent_const_art_038.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_038.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 38 - State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall strive to promote welfare of people by securing a social order informed by social, economic, and political justice, and minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: The constitutional mandate for a democratic socialist welfare state. Clause (2) was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Operationalizes the Preamble's commitment to social and economic justice.

parent_const_art_039.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_039.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 39 - Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Directs state policy to secure adequate means of livelihood, equitable distribution of community resources (39b), prevention of wealth concentration (39c), equal pay for equal work (39d), worker health, and child protection.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) enjoy special constitutional shielding under Article 31C. They form the basis of agrarian reforms, nationalization acts, and equal pay jurisprudence.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Clause (f) was modified by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

parent_const_art_039a.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
parent_const_art_039a.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_039a.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 39A - Equal justice and free legal aid
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall secure that legal system promotes justice on basis of equal opportunity and provide free legal aid to ensure justice is not denied by economic disability.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Led directly to the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 establishing NALSA, Lok Adalats, and free legal aid for undertrials and marginalized citizens. Read into Article 21 in Hussainara Khatoon (1979).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 based on Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer Committee recommendations.

parent_const_art_040.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_040.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 40 - Organisation of village panchayats
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with powers and authority to function as units of self-government.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Gandhian constitutional principle materialized decades later through the historic 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 enacting Part IX.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Debated intensely between Gandhian delegates and centralists in the Constituent Assembly.

parent_const_art_041.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_041.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 41 - Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall, within limits of economic capacity, secure right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutional inspiration for social security schemes, pensions, and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Reflects social democratic welfare obligations subject to state fiscal capacity.

parent_const_art_042.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_042.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 42 - Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guarantees occupational safety and maternity entitlements, underpinning the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and Factories Act, 1948.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Enforced by the Supreme Court in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000).

parent_const_art_043.title: Living wage, etc., for workers

ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 43 - Living wage, etc., for workers
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall endeavour to secure a living wage, decent standard of life, social/cultural opportunities, and promote cottage industries on individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Differentiates between bare subsistence wage, minimum wage, and living wage, establishing living wage as the ultimate state objective.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Combines industrial labour protection with Gandhian village cottage industry revival.

parent_const_art_044.title: Uniform civil code for the citizens
parent_const_art_044.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_044.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 44 - Uniform civil code for the citizens
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Directs the state toward common civil laws governing marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance, and adoption across religious communities. Highlighted by the Supreme Court in Shah Bano (1985) and Sarla Mudgal (1995).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Vigorously debated in the Constituent Assembly; placed in Part IV as a progressive long-term aspiration rather than an immediate enforceable right.

PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Refocused on early childhood care (0-6 years) after elementary education (6-14 years) was elevated to Article 21A.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Substituted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.

ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 46 - Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall promote educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and weaker sections, and protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutional anchor for affirmative welfare programs, scholarship schemes, and protective legislation for SC/ST communities.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Reflects the moral foundation behind Articles 15(4) and 16(4).

parent_const_art_047.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_047.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 47 - Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall regard raising nutrition, standard of living, and public health as primary duties, and endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and injurious drugs.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Primary constitutional source for public healthcare initiatives, National Food Security Act, and state alcohol prohibition laws.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Incorporated Gandhian prohibition ideals alongside public health commitments.

parent_const_art_048.title: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
parent_const_art_048.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_048.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 48 - Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines, improve breeds, and prohibit slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch/draught cattle.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Examined in State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005) upholding complete bans on cow progeny slaughter on agricultural and ecological grounds.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Reconciled scientific agricultural modernization with rural livestock preservation.

parent_const_art_048a.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_048a.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 48A - Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Cornerstone of Indian environmental law. Read together with Article 21 to create enforceable fundamental rights to clean water, pollution-free air, and ecological conservation (M.C. Mehta, Vellore Citizens).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 following India's commitments at the 1972 Stockholm Conference.

parent_const_art_049.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy

ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 49 - Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Obligation of State to protect monuments, places, and objects of national importance and artistic/historic interest from destruction, disfigurement, or export.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Underpins national heritage preservation acts and the Supreme Court's Taj Trapezium orders protecting the Taj Mahal.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Reflects commitment to safeguarding millennia of Indian civilization and cultural heritage.

parent_const_art_050.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 50 - Separation of judiciary from executive
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutional mandate for judicial independence, leading to the separation of judicial magistrates from executive magistrates in the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Dismantled colonial district magistrate systems where executive officers exercised judicial criminal powers.

parent_const_art_051.title: Promotion of international peace and security
parent_const_art_051.part: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
parent_const_art_051.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 51 - Promotion of international peace and security
PART: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy | CATEGORY: Directive Principle
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: State shall endeavour to promote international peace, maintain just relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaties, and encourage arbitration of international disputes.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guiding principle for Indian foreign policy. In Vishaka (1997), the Supreme Court used Article 51(c) to incorporate the CEDAW international convention into domestic law.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Drafted to articulate India's commitment to Panchsheel and the United Nations Charter.

parent_const_art_051a.title: Fundamental duties
parent_const_art_051a.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 51A - Fundamental duties
PART: Part IVA - Fundamental Duties | CATEGORY: Fundamental Duty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to: abide by Constitution and respect Flag/Anthem (a); cherish national struggle ideals (b); protect sovereignty and integrity (c); defend the country (d); promote brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to women (e); preserve composite culture (f); protect natural environment and wildlife (g); develop scientific temper and humanism (h); safeguard public property and abjure violence (i); strive for excellence (j); and provide education to child aged 6-14 (k).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Introduced by 42nd Amendment on Swaran Singh Committee recommendation. Clause (k) was added by 86th Amendment (2002). Non-justiciable directly, but used by courts to interpret constitutional provisions and validate reasonable restrictions.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inspired by the USSR Constitution, emphasizing that rights and duties are indivisible.

parent_const_art_052.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 52 - The President of India
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: There shall be a President of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes the highest constitutional office of the Republic as the formal Head of State.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Created a constitutional head of state under a parliamentary cabinet system.

parent_const_art_053.title: Executive power of the Union
parent_const_art_053.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 53 - Executive power of the Union
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Executive power of the Union is vested in the President, exercised directly or through subordinate officers. Supreme command of Defence Forces is vested in President.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: The President is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, exercising executive power subject to constitutional checks and ministerial advice.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Affirms civil supremacy over the military apparatus in independent India.

parent_const_art_061.title: Procedure for impeachment of the President
parent_const_art_061.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 61 - Procedure for impeachment of the President
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President may be impeached for violation of the Constitution. Charge preferred by either House with 14 days notice signed by 1/4th members, passed by 2/3rd majority of total membership of the House.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Quasi-judicial parliamentary impeachment mechanism with the highest voting threshold in the Constitution.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Designed to prevent partisan destabilization while checking gross unconstitutional actions.

parent_const_art_072.title: Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences
parent_const_art_072.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 72 - Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President has power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions, or suspend/commute sentences in court martial cases, offences under Union law, and all death sentences.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Executive clemency power. In Kehar Singh (1989) and Shatrughan Chauhan (2014), the Supreme Court ruled that clemency is exercised on aid and advice of Council of Ministers and is subject to limited judicial review for arbitrariness.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: A sovereign humane check against judicial error and excessive sentencing.

parent_const_art_074.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
parent_const_art_074.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 74 - Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: There shall be a Council of Ministers with Prime Minister at head to aid and advise President, who shall act in accordance with such advice. President may require reconsideration once. Ministerial advice is shielded from judicial inquiry.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Core clause of parliamentary cabinet democracy. The 42nd Amendment made ministerial advice strictly binding; the 44th Amendment added the proviso enabling the President to return advice once for reconsideration.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: In Samsher Singh (1974), the Supreme Court affirmed that the President is a constitutional head acting solely on ministerial advice.

parent_const_art_075.title: Other provisions as to Ministers
parent_const_art_075.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 75 - Other provisions as to Ministers
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Prime Minister appointed by President; other Ministers appointed on PM advice. Total Ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha (1A). Collective responsibility of Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha (3).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes collective responsibility as the vital link between legislature and executive. Clause (1A) was inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Codified Westminster conventions into written constitutional law.

parent_const_art_076.title: Attorney-General for India
parent_const_art_076.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 76 - Attorney-General for India
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President appoints person qualified to be Supreme Court judge as Attorney-General for India. Chief legal advisor to the Government of India with right of audience in all Indian courts.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Highest law officer of the country. Holds office during the pleasure of the President and has the right to speak in both Houses of Parliament without voting rights (Article 88).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Created an independent legal advisor modeled after the British Attorney General.

parent_const_art_105.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
parent_const_art_105.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 105 - Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Parliament
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Guarantees freedom of speech in Parliament. Absolute immunity of MPs from court proceedings for speech or votes in Parliament. In 2024, a 7-judge bench ruled bribery to cast a vote is not protected by Article 105 privileges.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Parliamentary privileges ensuring legislative independence. Overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) in Sita Soren (2024), clarifying that taking bribes to vote is not protected.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Traced to the English Bill of Rights 1689 ensuring parliamentary supremacy from royal prosecution.

parent_const_art_110.title: Definition of Money Bills
parent_const_art_110.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 110 - Definition of Money Bills
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Parliament
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Defines Money Bills dealing strictly with taxation, government borrowing, and Consolidated Fund appropriations. Speaker of Lok Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Money Bills cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha and Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend them. Examined in Puttaswamy (Aadhaar 2018) and Rojer Mathew (2019).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Vests financial supremacy exclusively in the directly elected popular house.

parent_const_art_123.title: Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
parent_const_art_123.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 123 - Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Executive
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President may promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament when circumstances require immediate action. Operates with force of Act, but lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Executive law-making power. In D.C. Wadhwa (1987) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), the Supreme Court ruled that re-promulgating ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Emergency legislative device derived from Section 72 of the Government of India Act 1935.

parent_const_art_123.explanation: Executive law-making power. In D.C. Wadhwa (1987) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), the Supreme Court ruled that re-promulgating ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution.
parent_const_art_123.historical_context: Emergency legislative device derived from Section 72 of the Government of India Act 1935.

parent_const_art_124.title: Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court
parent_const_art_124.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 124 - Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Establishes Supreme Court of India. Judges appointed by President after consultation with Chief Justice and Collegium, holding office until 65 years. Removal only through rigorous parliamentary impeachment for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: In Second Judges Case (1993) and Third Judges Case (1998), the Supreme Court evolved the Collegium System. In Fourth Judges Case (2015), the Court struck down the NJAC Act and 99th Amendment to protect judicial independence as a Basic Feature.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Replaced the Federal Court of India and Privy Council as the apex court of the land on January 28, 1950.

parent_const_art_129.title: Supreme Court to be a court of record
parent_const_art_129.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 129 - Supreme Court to be a court of record
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Supreme Court shall be a court of record and shall have all powers of such a court including power to punish for contempt of itself.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in subordinate courts. The inherent power to punish for contempt cannot be curtailed by ordinary legislation.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Essential attribute of sovereign superior courts.

parent_const_art_131.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 131 - Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Exclusive original jurisdiction of Supreme Court in federal disputes between Union and States or between States involving legal rights.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Federal arbitration mechanism for constitutional inter-governmental disputes.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Preserves federal equilibrium and peaceful constitutional dispute resolution.

parent_const_art_136.title: Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
parent_const_art_136.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 136 - Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Supreme Court may in its discretion grant special leave to appeal (SLP) against any judgment, decree, sentence or order of any court or tribunal in India (except armed forces tribunals).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction to remedy substantial injustice, making the Supreme Court accessible beyond formal statutory appellate pathways.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inherited and expanded from the Privy Council's historic royal prerogative jurisdiction.

parent_const_art_137.title: Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
parent_const_art_137.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 137 - Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Supreme Court has power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it, subject to parliamentary laws and rules of court.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Enables the Court to correct patent errors on the face of the record. Led to the innovative creation of Curative Petitions in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Essential safety valve against judicial infallibility in final appellate determinations.

parent_const_art_141.title: Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
parent_const_art_141.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 141 - Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutionalizes the common law doctrine of stare decisis (judicial precedent). Ratio decidendi declared by the Supreme Court operates as binding law nationwide, though the Supreme Court is not bound by its own previous decisions (Bengal Immunity, 1955).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Derived from Section 212 of the Government of India Act 1935, cementing judicial unity across the Republic.

parent_const_art_142.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 142 - Enforcement of decrees and orders of Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc.
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Supreme Court may pass decrees and orders necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter, enforceable throughout India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Extraordinary equitable power to bridge statutory vacuums and ensure complete justice. Used in Bhopal Gas disaster settlement (1991), Ayodhya title dispute (2019), and judicial guideline frameworks.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Vests inherent sovereign justice power in India's apex judicial authority.

parent_const_art_143.title: Power of President to consult Supreme Court
parent_const_art_143.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 143 - Power of President to consult Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President may consult Supreme Court on questions of law or public importance for advisory opinion (Presidential Reference).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Advisory jurisdiction. Opinions delivered under Article 143 are not binding judgments under Article 141, but carry authoritative persuasive weight (e.g. Berubari 1960, Special Courts Bill 1978, 2G Spectrum Reference 2012).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Modeled after Section 4 of the Judicial Committee Act 1833 and Canadian Supreme Court reference jurisdiction.

ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 144 - Civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court
PART: Part V - The Union | CATEGORY: Union Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Mandates full executive and bureaucratic compliance with Supreme Court orders and judgments throughout the nation.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Ensures decrees of the apex court are not frustrated by state non-compliance.

PART: Part VI - The States | CATEGORY: State Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: There shall be a High Court for each State.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Establishes High Courts as the apex judicial bodies within States.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inherited from the Indian High Courts Act 1861 establishing chartered High Courts in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.

CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: High Courts are courts of record with power to punish for contempt of itself.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Direct institutional descendant of sovereign colonial charter courts.

parent_const_art_226.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
parent_const_art_226.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 226 - Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
PART: Part VI - The States | CATEGORY: State Judiciary
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: High Courts have power to issue writs of Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose'.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Wider writ jurisdiction than Article 32 because 'for any other purpose' empowers High Courts to enforce ordinary statutory and legal rights. In L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the Supreme Court ruled that Article 226 judicial review is part of the Basic Structure.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Democratized constitutional remedies across all states of the Union.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Vests High Courts with institutional leadership over the state judicial hierarchy.

parent_const_art_245.part: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States

ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 245 - Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
PART: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States | CATEGORY: Legislative Relations
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament may make laws for the whole of India; State Legislatures make laws for the State. Parliamentary laws valid with extra-territorial operation.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Demarcates territorial legislative competency and establishes plenary extra-territorial powers of the Union Parliament.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Subject to constitutional limitations including Fundamental Rights and federal distribution of powers.

parent_const_art_246.part: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States
parent_const_art_246.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 246 - Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
PART: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States | CATEGORY: Legislative Relations
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Federal division of legislative powers: Parliament has exclusive power over Union List (List I); States have exclusive power over State List (List II); both have concurrent power over Concurrent List (List III).
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Core federal distribution interpreted through the Doctrine of Pith and Substance and Doctrine of Colourable Legislation.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Derived from the threefold legislative division in the Government of India Act 1935.

parent_const_art_248.part: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States
parent_const_art_248.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 248 - Residuary powers of legislation
PART: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States | CATEGORY: Legislative Relations
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Parliament has exclusive residuary legislative powers over any subject not enumerated in Concurrent List or State List.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Unlike the US or Australian federations where residuary power belongs to the states, the Indian Constitution deliberately vests residuary power in the Union Parliament.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Framed to ensure a strong Union equipped to address unforeseen future technological and socio-economic challenges.

parent_const_art_254.part: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States
parent_const_art_254.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 254 - Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States
PART: Part XI - Relations Between the Union and the States | CATEGORY: Legislative Relations
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Doctrine of Repugnancy: Parliamentary law prevails over State law in Concurrent List matters. Exception: State law prevails if reserved for and assented to by the President.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Resolves legislative conflicts between Centre and States in Concurrent List subjects, interpreted in M. Karunanidhi (1979) and Hoechst Pharmaceuticals (1983).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Ensures national uniformity in concurrent legal fields while permitting state-level innovation upon presidential assent.

parent_const_art_265.part: Part XII - Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits
parent_const_art_265.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 265 - Taxes not to be imposed save by authority of law
PART: Part XII - Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits | CATEGORY: Finance
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Guarantees no taxation without statutory authorization. Prohibits executive imposition of taxes by administrative circulars or executive fiat.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Democratic republican principle traced to Magna Carta and the English Petition of Right 1628.

parent_const_art_300a.part: Part XII - Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits
parent_const_art_300a.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 300A - Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law
PART: Part XII - Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits | CATEGORY: Property
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Constitutional right to property following its repeal from Fundamental Rights. In Vidya Devi (2020) and Kolkata Municipal Corporation (2024), the Supreme Court ruled that Article 300A is a human right requiring fair compensation and procedure.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, which deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.

parent_const_art_352.title: Proclamation of Emergency
parent_const_art_352.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 352 - Proclamation of Emergency
PART: Part XVIII - Emergency Provisions | CATEGORY: Emergency
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President may proclaim National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. Requires written advice of Union Cabinet and parliamentary approval by special majority within one month.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: The 44th Amendment replaced vague 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' and added the safeguard of written Cabinet communication and special majority approval.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: National Emergency declared in 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war), and 1975-77 (internal emergency).

parent_const_art_356.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 356 - Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States (President's Rule)
PART: Part XVIII - Emergency Provisions | CATEGORY: Emergency
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: President may impose President's Rule in a State upon failure of constitutional machinery, assuming executive functions and conferring legislative powers on Parliament.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Heavily debated provision. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a 9-judge bench ruled that proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, floor tests are mandatory, and secularism is part of the Basic Structure.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Dr. Ambedkar hoped Article 356 would remain a 'dead letter', but it was invoked over 100 times prior to Bommai.

parent_const_art_368.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor
parent_const_art_368.part: Part XX - Amendment of the Constitution
parent_const_art_368.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 368 - Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor
PART: Part XX - Amendment of the Constitution | CATEGORY: Constitutional Amendments
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
(2) An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament...
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 368 lays down the procedure and power of Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, as declared in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 is not absolute and cannot be exercised to alter, damage, or destroy the 'Basic Structure' or foundational features of the Constitution.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Central to major constitutional battles between Parliament and the Judiciary, culminating in the doctrine of Basic Structure.

parent_const_art_370.title: Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir
parent_const_art_370.part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
parent_const_art_370.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 370 - Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir
PART: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions | CATEGORY: Special Provisions
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: Temporary provisions granting special autonomous status to the State of Jammu and Kashmir within the Indian Union, restricting Parliament's legislative powers over J&K to Defence, External Affairs, and Communications unless concurred by the J&K Constituent Assembly.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 370 granted special status to J&K. In August 2019, Presidential Orders (C.O. 272 and C.O. 273) and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act effectively rendered Article 370 inoperative and reorganized J&K into Union Territories. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of this abrogation in December 2023.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Incorporated in 1949 as a temporary provision following the Instrument of Accession signed by Maharaja Hari Singh.

parent_amend_001.title: The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951
parent_amend_001.full_text:
AMENDMENT: 1st Constitutional Amendment Act (1951)
TITLE: The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951
PROVISIONS MODIFIED: Article 15(4), Article 19(2), Article 31A, Article 31B, Ninth Schedule
SUMMARY: Added Article 15(4) enabling affirmative action reservations following Champakam Dorairajan; added 'public order', 'friendly relations with foreign states', and 'incitement to an offence' as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2); created Ninth Schedule and Article 31B to protect agrarian land reforms from judicial review.
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS: To overcome judicial decisions invalidating state laws regarding land reform, zamindari abolition, and affirmative action, and to introduce reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech in the interest of public order.

parent_amend_024.title: The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971
parent_amend_024.full_text:
AMENDMENT: 24th Constitutional Amendment Act (1971)
TITLE: The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971
PROVISIONS MODIFIED: Article 13(4), Article 368
SUMMARY: Affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, by inserting Article 13(4) and amending Article 368. Made presidential assent to constitutional amendment bills mandatory.
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS: Enacted in response to the Supreme Court's ruling in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), which held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights under Article 368.

parent_amend_025.title: The Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971

AMENDMENT: 25th Constitutional Amendment Act (1971)
TITLE: The Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971
PROVISIONS MODIFIED: Article 31(2), Article 31C
SUMMARY: Substituted the word 'amount' for 'compensation' under Article 31(2) and inserted Article 31C providing that laws giving effect to Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged under Articles 14, 19, or 31.
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS: To overcome the Supreme Court ruling in R.C. Cooper (Bank Nationalisation case) regarding market-value compensation for acquired property and to advance socio-economic directive principles.

parent_amend_042.title: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (Mini-Constitution)
parent_amend_042.full_text:
AMENDMENT: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976)
TITLE: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (Mini-Constitution)
PROVISIONS MODIFIED: Preamble, Article 31C, Article 39A, Article 43A, Article 48A, Part IVA (Article 51A), Article 74, Article 368(4)-(5)
SUMMARY: Added 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble; introduced Part IVA Fundamental Duties (Article 51A); added Directive Principles on free legal aid (39A), workers participation (43A), and environment (48A); made Council of Ministers advice strictly binding on the President; attempted to make constitutional amendments completely immune from judicial review (later struck down in Minerva Mills).
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS: Comprehensive overhaul based on the Swaran Singh Committee recommendations to assert parliamentary supremacy and implement socio-economic directives during the Emergency.

parent_amend_044.title: The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978
parent_amend_044.full_text:
AMENDMENT: 44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978)
TITLE: The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978
PROVISIONS MODIFIED: Article 19(1)(f), Article 31, Article 300A, Article 74, Article 352, Article 359
SUMMARY: Restored civil liberties post-Emergency; deleted Right to Property from Fundamental Rights (repealing 19(1)(f) and 31) and reclassified it as a constitutional right under Article 300A; substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance' in Article 352; mandated written Cabinet advice for declaring Emergency; prohibited suspension of Articles 20 and 21 even during National Emergency under Article 359.
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS: Enacted by the Janata Government to dismantle Emergency-era constitutional distortions and safeguard fundamental democratic rights against executive tyranny.

parent_case_sc_kesavananda_1973.case_name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
parent_case_sc_kesavananda_1973.full_text:
CASE NAME: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala (1973)
CITATION: (1973) 4 SCC 225 | BENCH: 13-Judge Bench (7:6 Majority)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 368, Article 13, Article 31C, Preamble
FACTS: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act which restricted religious mutt property ownership, challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments under Article 368.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Parliament has wide constituent amending power under Article 368 but cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Indian Constitution. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
VERDICT: Upheld 24th Amendment; partially struck down Article 31C; established the landmark Basic Structure Doctrine.
KEY TAKEAWAYS:

CASE NAME: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India (1951)
CITATION: AIR 1951 SC 458 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 13, Article 31A, Article 31B, Article 368
FACTS: Landowners challenged the validity of the First Amendment, which inserted Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule, arguing it curtailed Fundamental Rights under Part III in violation of Article 13(2).
RATIO DECIDENDI: 'Law' in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislative enactments and not to constituent amendments made under Article 368. Parliament can amend any provision including Fundamental Rights.
VERDICT: Upheld the validity of the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.

CASE NAME: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965)

ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 13, Article 31A, Article 368
FACTS: Challenge to the 17th Amendment Act which added diverse State land reform acts into the Ninth Schedule.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Affirmed Shankari Prasad ruling that Parliament's amending power extends to Fundamental Rights. However, Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar expressed profound doubts whether Fundamental Rights could be stripped away.
VERDICT: Upheld 17th Amendment, but sowed the conceptual seeds for Golak Nath and Basic Structure.

acts_referred: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
parent_case_sc_golak_nath_1967.full_text:
CASE NAME: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967)
CITATION: AIR 1967 SC 1643 | BENCH: 11-Judge Bench (6:5 Majority)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 13(2), Article 368, Article 19(1)(f), Article 31
FACTS: Family of Golak Nath held 500 acres of land. State declared excess land surplus under land reforms act. Family challenged 17th Amendment as abridging fundamental property rights.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Fundamental Rights hold a transcendental and immutable position. Constitutional amendments under Article 368 are 'law' under Article 13(2). Parliament has no power to abridge Fundamental Rights. Applied Doctrine of Prospective Overruling.
VERDICT: Held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; prospectively applied to save past amendments.

parent_case_sc_indira_gandhi_1975.case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
parent_case_sc_indira_gandhi_1975.full_text:
CASE NAME: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
CITATION: AIR 1975 SC 2299 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 329A, Article 14, Article 368
FACTS: Allahabad High Court invalidated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's election for corrupt electoral practices. Parliament enacted the 39th Amendment inserting Article 329A(4) placing election of PM and Speaker beyond judicial review.
RATIO DECIDENDI: First direct application of Basic Structure Doctrine. Democracy, rule of law, equality (Article 14), and judicial review are basic features. A constitutional amendment placing an individual's election beyond judicial scrutiny violates the Basic Structure.
VERDICT: Struck down Article 329A(4) inserted by the 39th Amendment; upheld election on statutory merits.

parent_case_sc_minerva_mills_1980.case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
parent_case_sc_minerva_mills_1980.full_text:
CASE NAME: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
CITATION: (1980) 3 SCC 625 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (4:1 Majority)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 368(4), Article 368(5), Article 31C, Article 14, Article 19, Part III, Part IV
FACTS: Minerva Mills challenged nationalization and the 42nd Amendment which added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 asserting unlimited amending power and expanded Article 31C to subordinate Fundamental Rights to all Directive Principles.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot convert limited power into unlimited power. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential basic feature.
VERDICT: Struck down Section 55 (Article 368(4)-(5)) and Section 4 (blanket Article 31C) of 42nd Amendment.

parent_case_sc_ir_coelho_2007.case_name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu
parent_case_sc_ir_coelho_2007.full_text:
CASE NAME: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
CITATION: (2007) 2 SCC 1 | BENCH: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 9:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 31B, Ninth Schedule, Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Article 32
FACTS: Referred to 9-judge bench to definitively resolve whether statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda Bharati are completely immunized from judicial review for violating Fundamental Rights.
RATIO DECIDENDI: All laws placed in Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review using the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test'. If a Ninth Schedule statute violates the principles underlying Articles 14, 19, or 21, it damages the Basic Structure and will be void.
VERDICT: Unanimously affirmed that Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a constitutional black hole to bypass the Basic Structure.

parent_case_sc_ak_gopalan_1950.case_name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
parent_case_sc_ak_gopalan_1950.full_text:
CASE NAME: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
CITATION: AIR 1950 SC 27 | BENCH: 6-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19, Article 21, Article 22
FACTS: Communist leader A.K. Gopalan was detained under Preventive Detention Act without trial. He claimed detention infringed freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d) and personal liberty under Article 21.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Adopted narrow literal interpretation. 'Procedure established by law' means state-enacted statutory law, not natural justice. Articles 19 and 21 operate in mutually exclusive silos; preventive detention does not attract Article 19. (Justice Fazl Ali dissented).
VERDICT: Upheld Preventive Detention Act; rejected substantive due process.
KEY TAKEAWAYS:

parent_case_sc_maneka_gandhi_1978.full_text:
CASE NAME: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
CITATION: (1978) 1 SCC 248 | BENCH: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(1)(g)
FACTS: Regional Passport Office impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport 'in public interest' without furnishing reasons or providing a hearing.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Overruled Gopalan's silo approach; established the 'Golden Triangle' of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Any procedure depriving life or personal liberty must be 'just, fair, and reasonable' and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty.
VERDICT: Substantive and procedural due process integrated into Article 21; audi alteram partem mandated.
