CITATION: (1978) 4 SCC 494 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Article 32
FACTS: Death-row convict Sunil Batra challenged solitary confinement and inhumane bar fetters in Tihar Jail prior to disposal of appeals.

CASE NAME: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979)
CITATION: (1980) 1 SCC 81 | BENCH: 3-Judge Bench (Justice P.N. Bhagwati)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 39A
FACTS: Kapila Hingorani filed PIL highlighting tens of thousands of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails for periods exceeding maximum statutory sentences awaiting trial.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Right to speedy trial is an integral fundamental right under Article 21. Depriving indigent accused of legal representation violates fair procedure. Ordered immediate release of undertrials whose detention exceeded maximum sentences.
VERDICT: First landmark PIL in Indian legal history; released over 40,000 undertrials; established right to speedy trial and legal aid.

FACTS: British national detained under COFEPOSA was denied permission to meet family members and legal counsel under stringent prison restrictions.

CASE NAME: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
CITATION: (1997) 1 SCC 416 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 22
FACTS: PIL petition letter by Executive Chairman, Legal Aid Services West Bengal, drawing attention to frequent custodial deaths and police brutality.

Formulated 11 binding guidelines (memo of arrest, informing relative, medical examination every 48 hours, right to meet lawyer, display at control room) that must be strictly observed during arrest and detention.

parent_case_sc_aruna_shanbaug_2011.full_text:
CASE NAME: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011)
CITATION: (2011) 4 SCC 454 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench (Justice Markandey Katju)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21
FACTS: Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse at KEM Hospital Mumbai, remained in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for 37 years following a brutal sexual assault. Journalist Pinki Virani filed a writ petition seeking withdrawal of life support.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Differentiated active euthanasia (administering lethal injection, prohibited) from passive euthanasia (withholding artificial life-support). Legalized passive euthanasia subject to strict High Court approval and medical board evaluation under the parens patriae doctrine.
VERDICT: Permitted passive euthanasia under judicial supervision; declined withdrawal for Aruna as KEM staff wished to care for her.

CASE NAME: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India (2018)
CITATION: (2018) 5 SCC 1 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (CJI Dipak Misra)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21
FACTS: Common Cause filed PIL seeking legal recognition of 'living wills' (advance medical directives) enabling terminally ill patients to refuse artificial life prolongation.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of the fundamental right to live with dignity under Article 21. An adult person of sound mind has bodily autonomy to execute an Advance Medical Directive refusing artificial life support when death is imminent.
VERDICT: Unanimously recognized Living Wills and advance medical directives; laid down simplified procedural safeguards.

CASE NAME: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954)
CITATION: AIR 1954 SC 300 | BENCH: 8-Judge Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19(1)(f), Article 20(3)
FACTS: Search warrants issued in Dalmia Group fraud investigation. Petitioners claimed search and seizure of private documents violated Article 19(1)(f) and Article 20(3).

CITATION: (1994) 6 SCC 632 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench (Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19(1)(a), Article 21
FACTS: Condemned prisoner Auto Shankar wrote an autobiography disclosing unholy nexus with high-ranking police and prison officials. Prison authorities threatened publisher Nakkheeran with legal action to suppress publication.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Right to privacy is implicit in Article 21 ('right to be let alone'). A citizen has a right to safeguard the privacy of his family, marriage, procreation, and education. Public officials cannot suppress publication or claim damages for defamation unless statements are made with reckless disregard for truth.
VERDICT: Permitted publication; established tort of invasion of privacy and American New York Times v. Sullivan public official standard in India.

parent_case_sc_puttaswamy_privacy_2017.case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment)
parent_case_sc_puttaswamy_privacy_2017.full_text:
CASE NAME: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment) (2017)
CITATION: (2017) 10 SCC 1 | BENCH: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 9:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19, Part III
FACTS: Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the mandatory Aadhaar biometric identification program. The Attorney General argued that under M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1963), the Constitution guaranteed no fundamental right to privacy.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Privacy is an intrinsic, fundamental, and inalienable right emanating from life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the entire schema of Part III. Privacy encompasses bodily autonomy, informational privacy, and spatial privacy. Any state interference must pass the three-fold test of: (1) legality (state law), (2) legitimate state aim, and (3) proportionality.
VERDICT: Unanimously upheld Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21; overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise; explicitly denounced ADM Jabalpur.

parent_case_sc_shreya_singhal_2015.case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
parent_case_sc_shreya_singhal_2015.full_text:
CASE NAME: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
CITATION: (2015) 5 SCC 1 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench (Justices J. Chelameswar & R.F. Nariman)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Article 14
FACTS: Two girls were arrested in Maharashtra under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting comments on Facebook questioning the city shutdown for Bal Thackeray's funeral. Law student Shreya Singhal filed a PIL challenging Section 66A.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Section 66A created a chilling effect on free online speech. Differentiated between discussion, advocacy, and incitement. A speech becomes restriction-worthy under Article 19(2) only when it reaches the level of incitement. The terms 'grossly offensive' and 'annoying' were hopelessly vague. Read down Section 79 intermediary guidelines to require court orders or government notifications for takedowns.
VERDICT: Struck down Section 66A IT Act in its entirety as unconstitutional; protected internet freedom in India.

CITATION: (2020) 3 SCC 637 | BENCH: 3-Judge Bench (Justice N.V. Ramana)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(1)(g), Article 19(2), Article 21
FACTS: Following the revocation of Article 370 in August 2019, the government imposed indefinite internet shutdown and movement restrictions under Section 144 CrPC across Jammu and Kashmir. Editor of Kashmir Times challenged the blackout.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)) and freedom to carry on trade/business (Article 19(1)(g)) using the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected fundamental rights. VERDICT: Declared internet access constitutionally protected; prohibited indefinite shutdowns; mandated periodic review.

parent_case_sc_champakam_1951.case_name: State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan
parent_case_sc_champakam_1951.full_text:
CASE NAME: State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
CITATION: AIR 1951 SC 226 | BENCH: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 15(1), Article 29(2), Article 46
FACTS: Madras Government issued a Communal G.O. allocating medical and engineering college seats based strictly on caste and religious quotas. Brahmin student Champakam Dorairajan challenged the order after denial of admission.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be overridden by Directive Principles in Part IV. The Communal G.O. classified candidates solely on religion and caste, directly violating Article 29(2).
VERDICT: Struck down Communal G.O.; prompted Parliament to enact the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserting Article 15(4).

CITATION: (1974) 4 SCC 3 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Justice P.N. Bhagwati)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 14, Article 16
FACTS: Senior IAS officer E.P. Royappa was transferred from the post of Chief Secretary to a newly created non-cadre post, which he challenged as arbitrary, malicious, and violative of Articles 14 and 16.

Where an act is arbitrary, it implicitly involves negation of equality.
VERDICT: Established the anti-arbitrariness principle as the foundational bedrock of Article 14.

parent_case_sc_indra_sawhney_1992.full_text:
CASE NAME: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case) (1992)
CITATION: 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217 | BENCH: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (6:3 Majority)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 16(4), Article 14, Article 15(4), Article 335
FACTS: V.P. Singh government implemented the Mandal Commission report reserving 27% vacancies in central civil services for Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Petitioners challenged the policy.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4). Caste can be an acceptable starting point for identifying backwardness. Established the 'Creamy Layer' exclusion principle for advanced sections of OBCs. Imposed a strict 50% ceiling on total reservations. Stated reservation applies only to initial appointments and not to promotions.
VERDICT: Upheld OBC reservation with creamy layer exclusion and 50% cap; prohibited reservation in promotions.

VERDICT: Upheld 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th Amendments subject to quantifiable data and efficiency requirements.

CITATION: (1986) 3 SCC 615 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench (Justice O. Chinnappa Reddy)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 19(1)(a), Article 25(1), Article 51A(a)
FACTS: Three school children belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses stood respectfully when the National Anthem was sung in school assembly, but did not sing along due to conscientious religious tenets. They were expelled.

VERDICT: Quashed expulsion; held our tradition teaches tolerance, our philosophy preaches tolerance, our Constitution practices tolerance.

CITATION: (1985) 2 SCC 556 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (CJI Y.V. Chandrachud)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 44, Article 14, Article 21
FACTS: 62-year-old divorced Muslim woman Shah Bano sought maintenance from her wealthy advocate husband under Section 125 CrPC. The husband argued Muslim personal law limited maintenance to the iddat period.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, compassionate statutory measure designed to prevent destitution and vagrancy. It applies to all citizens regardless of religion. It overrides personal laws where a divorced wife is unable to maintain herself. Highlighted the necessity of a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44).
VERDICT: Awarded maintenance to Shah Bano; affirmed secular primacy of Section 125 CrPC.

ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 14, Article 15, Article 19(1)(a), Article 21
FACTS: LGBTQ+ activists challenged Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized consensual sexual acts 'against the order of nature', following the retrograde reversal in Suresh Koushal (2013).

VERDICT: Decriminalized consensual homosexual sex by reading down Section 377; recognized constitutional morality.

parent_case_sc_joseph_shine_2018.full_text:
CASE NAME: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery) (2018)
CITATION: (2019) 3 SCC 39 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 5:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 14, Article 15(1), Article 21
FACTS: Non-resident Indian Joseph Shine filed PIL challenging Section 497 IPC which punished a man for adultery with a married woman without consent of her husband, treating the woman as chattel of her husband.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Section 497 IPC is based on archaic patriarchal stereotypes reducing women to the chattel of their husbands. It punishes the outsider man while treating the woman as an object without agency, violating Article 14 and Article 15. Matrimonial infidelity is a civil ground for divorce, not a criminal offence under state penal sanctions.
VERDICT: Unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC as unconstitutional.
KEY TAKEAWAYS:

parent_case_sc_first_judges_1981.case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case)

CASE NAME: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case) (1981)
CITATION: 1981 Supp SCC 87 | BENCH: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 124, Article 217, Article 222
FACTS: Challenge to government circular on non-appointment of additional High Court judges and mass transfers of High Court judges without concurrence of Chief Justice of India.
RATIO DECIDENDI: 'Consultation' does not mean 'concurrence'. The executive holds primacy in judicial appointments and transfers, provided there is full and effective consultation. Also established expansive rules of locus standi for Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
VERDICT: Executive held primacy in judicial appointments (later overruled in Second Judges Case); liberalized PIL locus standi.

CASE NAME: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case / Fourth Judges) (2015)

CITATION: (1997) 3 SCC 261 | BENCH: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 7:0)

parent_case_sc_sr_bommai_1994.case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
parent_case_sc_sr_bommai_1994.full_text:
CASE NAME: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
CITATION: (1994) 3 SCC 1 | BENCH: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 356, Article 74(2), Article 355, Preamble
FACTS: Dismissal of multiple State governments (Karnataka, Meghalaya, Nagaland, and BJP-ruled governments in MP, Rajasthan, HP following Babri Masjid demolition) under Article 356 President's Rule.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review for mala fides or irrelevant grounds. Secularism and Federalism are Basic Features of the Constitution. Floor test on the floor of the Legislative Assembly is the only constitutional forum for testing majority. State Assembly cannot be dissolved until both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation.
VERDICT: Restored dismissed assemblies; placed strict constitutional checks on Article 356 abuse.

parent_case_sc_rameshwar_prasad_2006.full_text:
CASE NAME: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (Bihar Assembly Dissolution) (2006)
CITATION: (2006) 2 SCC 1 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 356, Article 361
FACTS: Following inconclusive Bihar assembly elections in 2005, the Governor sent a midnight report claiming horse-trading, prompting the Union Cabinet to recommend dissolution of the newly elected assembly before its first meeting.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Dissolution of the assembly based on subjective suspicion of horse-trading without permitting a floor test is unconstitutional and mala fide. A Governor cannot scuttle the constitutional process of government formation based on personal conjectures.
VERDICT: Held midnight dissolution unconstitutional; affirmed strict compliance with Bommai floor test.

ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 239AA, Article 74
FACTS: Dispute between elected Delhi Government (Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal) and the Lieutenant Governor (LG) regarding administrative primacy and control over governance in the National Capital.

parent_case_sc_punjab_governor_2023.case_name: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab
parent_case_sc_punjab_governor_2023.full_text:
CASE NAME: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab (2023)
CITATION: (2023) 14 SCC 285 | BENCH: 3-Judge Bench (CJI D.Y. Chandrachud)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 200, Article 174
FACTS: Governor of Punjab refused to grant assent to multiple bills passed by the Vidhan Sabha, claiming the speaker's reconvening of the budget session was illegal and withholding assent indefinitely.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Governors cannot sit indefinitely on bills passed by elected state legislatures. Under Article 200, if a Governor decides to withhold assent, he must return the bill to the legislature 'as soon as possible' for reconsideration. A Governor is a symbolic constitutional head and cannot veto democratic legislation.
VERDICT: Mandated that Governors act promptly; prohibited indefinite pocket-vetoes of state legislation.

CITATION: (2024) 4 SCC 1 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 5:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 370, Article 356, Article 3, Article 1
FACTS: Challenge to the abrogating Presidential Orders C.O. 272 and C.O. 273 of August 2019 which rendered Article 370 inoperative and bifurcated Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Article 370 was a temporary transitional provision intended to facilitate constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir into the Indian Union. Upon signing the Instrument of Accession, J&K retained no internal sovereignty. The President had the power to issue notifications declaring Article 370 inoperative.
VERDICT: Unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of abrogating Article 370; directed statehood restoration and elections by September 2024.

parent_case_sc_mc_mehta_oleum_1987.full_text:
CASE NAME: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987)
CITATION: (1987) 1 SCC 395 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (CJI P.N. Bhagwati)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 32
FACTS: Severe leak of hazardous Oleum gas from Shriram Foods and Fertilizer plant in Delhi shortly after the Bhopal disaster, causing deaths and mass panic. M.C. Mehta filed PIL under Article 32.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Evolved the landmark 'Absolute Liability' doctrine, discarding the 19th-century English Rylands v. Fletcher strict liability with its exceptions. An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and financial capacity of the enterprise.
VERDICT: Established Absolute Liability in Indian tort and constitutional jurisprudence.

CASE NAME: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (Span Motels Case) (1997)
CITATION: (1997) 1 SCC 388 | BENCH: 2-Judge Bench (Justice Kuldip Singh)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 48A
FACTS: Span Motels, owned by family of former Union Minister Kamal Nath, diverted the natural course of the Beas River in Himachal Pradesh to build a commercial luxury resort.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Incorporated the 'Public Trust Doctrine' into Indian jurisprudence. The state is the trustee of all natural resources (rivers, forests, seashores, air) for the public benefit and cannot convert public trust lands into private commercial exploitation.
VERDICT: Quashed leases; ordered motel management to pay exemplary pollution damages and restore river course.

CASE NAME: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case) (1985)
CITATION: (1985) 3 SCC 545 | BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (CJI Y.V. Chandrachud)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 19(1)(e), Article 39(a)
FACTS: BMC initiated eviction of pavement and slum dwellers from Bombay footpaths without notice or alternative rehabilitation during monsoon rains.
RATIO DECIDENDI: The right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21. If the right to livelihood is not treated as part of the right to life, the easiest way of depriving a person of his life would be to deprive him of his means of livelihood. Eviction cannot be executed without notice and reasonable opportunity of being heard.
VERDICT: Recognized Right to Livelihood in Article 21; mandated fair notice and phased alternative housing.

FACTS: Widespread starvation deaths occurred in Rajasthan while Food Corporation of India (FCI) godowns were overflowing with rotting grain.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Right to food is an indispensable component of Article 21. In a welfare state, preventing starvation is a non-negotiable state duty. Converted executive welfare schemes into justiciable legal entitlements, mandating mid-day meals in all government primary schools.
VERDICT: Mandated universal school Mid-Day Meal Scheme; led to the National Food Security Act, 2013.

CITATION: (2024) 5 SCC 625 | BENCH: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 7:0, CJI D.Y. Chandrachud)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 105(2), Article 194(2)
FACTS: JMM MLA Sita Soren was accused of accepting a bribe to vote for an independent candidate in Rajya Sabha elections. She claimed constitutional immunity under Article 194(2) relying on P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
RATIO DECIDENDI: Parliamentary privilege under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) exists to foster deliberative democratic independence, not to confer exemption from ordinary criminal law. The crime of bribery is complete the moment the bribe is accepted, irrespective of whether the vote is subsequently cast.
VERDICT: Unanimously overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao; held legislators taking bribes enjoy no immunity from prosecution.

parent_const_art_12.title: Definition of 'State'
parent_const_art_12.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 12 - Definition of 'State'
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Fundamental Rights
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 12 defines 'the State' specifically for the purpose of Fundamental Rights under Part III. Fundamental Rights are primarily enforceable against the State. The term 'other authorities' has been judicially expanded to include statutory bodies, government corporations, and agencies performing public functions (e.g., electricity boards, public universities, ONGC).
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Created to ensure clear accountability of government bodies and state instrumentalities when citizens claim fundamental rights violations.

parent_const_art_14.title: Equality before law
parent_const_art_14.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 14 - Equality before law
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Right to Equality
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 14 guarantees two concepts: 'Equality before law' (a negative concept derived from British law, meaning no one is above the law) and 'Equal protection of laws' (a positive concept derived from American law, permitting reasonable classification for differential treatment of equals). It prohibits arbitrary state action and strikes at discrimination.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Forms the bedrock of Indian democracy. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) and Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Supreme Court held that equality is a dynamic concept opposing arbitrariness.

parent_const_art_19.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
parent_const_art_19.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 19 - Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Right to Freedom
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: 1) All citizens shall have the right: (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business.
(2)-(6) The State may impose reasonable restrictions on these rights in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency, morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 19 guarantees six basic fundamental freedoms to Indian citizens. Crucially, these rights are not absolute; clauses (2) through (6) empower the legislature to enact 'reasonable restrictions' on defined grounds such as public order, national sovereignty, and security.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Subject to landmark amendments. The 1st Amendment Act (1951) added public order and friendly relations with foreign states as grounds for restrictions.

parent_const_art_21.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
parent_const_art_21.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 21 - Protection of life and personal liberty
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Right to Life & Personal Liberty
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 21 is the most broadly interpreted fundamental right in the Indian Constitution. Though framed as 'procedure established by law', the judiciary in Maneka Gandhi (1978) established that the procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable, effectively bringing Substantive Due Process into Indian jurisprudence. It encompasses the Right to Privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), Right to Clean Environment, Right to Dignified Life, Right to Free Legal Aid, and Right to Livelihood.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Initially interpreted narrowly in A.K. Gopalan (1950), but radically expanded post-Emergency in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and subsequent PIL decisions.

parent_const_art_21A.title: Right to Education
parent_const_art_21A.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 21A - Right to Education
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Right to Education
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Article 21A makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14. Enacted via the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, transforming a Directive Principle (Article 45) into an enforceable Fundamental Right following Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) decisions.

parent_const_art_32.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by Part III
parent_const_art_32.full_text:
ARTICLE/TITLE: Article 32 - Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by Part III
PART: Part III - Fundamental Rights | CATEGORY: Right to Constitutional Remedies
CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT: (1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.
(2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.
LEGAL EXPLANATION: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously referred to Article 32 as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. It guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights via five Constitutional Writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right and constitutes a cornerstone of Judicial Review and the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

parent_case_kesavananda.case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
parent_case_kesavananda.full_text:
CASE NAME: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
CITATION: (1973) 4 SCC 225 | BENCH: 13-Judge Bench (7:6 Majority)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 368, Article 13, Article 19, Article 31, Preamble
FACTS: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati, head of a Hindu Math in Kerala, challenged Kerala land reform acts under Article 26 (right to manage religiously owned property). During the pendency, Parliament passed the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendment Acts, restricting fundamental rights and asserting unlimited parliamentary amendment power.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Parliament has wide powers to amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368, including Fundamental Rights, BUT this power does not extend to altering, damaging, or destroying the 'Basic Structure' or core framework of the Constitution.
VERDICT: Upheld the validity of the 24th Amendment but invalidated parts of the 25th Amendment that sought to bypass judicial review. Established the Basic Structure Doctrine as a constitutional limitation on legislative power.
KEY TAKEAWAYS: Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution. Basic Structure includes Supremacy of Constitution, Republican & Democratic form of Government, Secularism, Separation of Powers, Federalism, and Judicial Review. Judicial review cannot be completely ousted by Constitutional Amendments.

parent_case_maneka.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
parent_case_maneka.full_text:
CASE NAME: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
CITATION: (1978) 1 SCC 248 | BENCH: 7-Judge Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19
FACTS: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the Regional Passport Office under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 in 'public interest'. The government refused to provide reasons for impounding her passport. She challenged this under Article 21.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Procedure established by law under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, oppressive, or fancy; it MUST be just, fair, and reasonable. Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive but form an interlinked 'Golden Triangle'.
VERDICT: Overruled the narrow interpretation of Article 21 in A.K. Gopalan (1950). The right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21. Natural justice (audi alteram partem) must be complied with.
KEY TAKEAWAYS: Integrated Due Process of Law into Indian Constitutional jurisprudence. Established the Golden Triangle concept (Articles 14, 19, and 21 must be read together). Transformed Article 21 into an expansive umbrella for human rights in India.

parent_case_puttaswamy.case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
parent_case_puttaswamy.full_text:
CASE NAME: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)
CITATION: (2017) 10 SCC 1 | BENCH: 9-Judge Bench (Unanimous 9:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19, Part III
FACTS: A challenge was brought against the Aadhaar biometric identification scheme. The government argued that the Indian Constitution does not explicitly guarantee a Fundamental Right to Privacy, relying on M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962). A 9-judge bench was constituted to settle the question of law.
RATIO DECIDENDI: The Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21 and forms part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. Privacy includes spatial privacy, informational privacy, and bodily autonomy.
VERDICT: Unanimously held that Privacy is a Fundamental Right. Any state intrusion into privacy must satisfy a 3-fold test: (1) Legality (backed by law), (2) Need / Legitimate State Aim, and (3) Proportionality.
KEY TAKEAWAYS: Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent they held privacy was not a fundamental right. Laid down the Proportionality Test for state interference in individual liberty. Paved the way for data protection legislation and decriminalization of Section 377 IPC.

parent_case_minerva.case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
parent_case_minerva.full_text:
CASE NAME: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
CITATION: (1980) 3 SCC 625 | BENCH: 5-Judge Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 368, Article 31C, Article 14, Article 19
FACTS: Minerva Mills, a textile company in Karnataka, was nationalized under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974. The petitioners challenged Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, which declared that no constitutional amendment could be questioned in any court and granted unlimited amendment power to Parliament.
RATIO DECIDENDI: A limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution. Parliament cannot give itself unlimited amending power under Article 368 to destroy the Basic Structure.
VERDICT: Struck down Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 (inserted by 42nd Amendment) and declared that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential basic feature.
KEY TAKEAWAYS: Re-affirmed and fortified the Basic Structure doctrine of Kesavananda Bharati. Held that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary like two wheels of a chariot. Restored judicial review as an unalterable basic feature.

parent_case_bommai.case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
parent_case_bommai.full_text:
CASE NAME: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
CITATION: (1994) 3 SCC 1 | BENCH: 9-Judge Bench
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 356, Article 352, Preamble
FACTS: Dismissal of Janata Dal government in Karnataka headed by S.R. Bommai and BJP governments in Rajasthan, MP, and HP under Article 356 (President's Rule). The President had dissolved state assemblies on arbitrary grounds.
RATIO DECIDENDI: Proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to Judicial Review. Secularism and Federalism are essential features of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
VERDICT: Laid down strict guidelines for invoking Article 356. The floor test in the Legislative Assembly is the sole legal test for determining majority, not the Governor's subjective opinion.
KEY TAKEAWAYS: Declared Secularism and Federalism as Basic Features of the Indian Constitution. Curbed political misuse of Article 356 by making Presidential proclamations subject to judicial scrutiny. Mandated floor test for proving majority of state governments.

parent_case_bommai.ratio_decidendi: Proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to Judicial Review. Secularism and Federalism are essential features of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
parent_case_bommai.verdict: Laid down strict guidelines for invoking Article 356. The floor test in the Legislative Assembly is the sole legal test for determining majority, not the Governor's subjective opinion.
key_takeaways: Declared Secularism and Federalism as Basic Features of the Indian Constitution.
Curbed political misuse of Article 356 by making Presidential proclamations subject to judicial scrutiny.
Mandated floor test for proving majority of state governments.
